title: Quality Assurance and Testing for ML
oneLiner: ML systems break through bad data, drift and hidden group failures, so test the data, the model, the system and the live rollout, not only the code.

what.html:
Quality assurance for ML checks every layer: is the data valid, does the pipeline run reliably, is the model good for every group of users, does the whole system work, and does the new model behave on real traffic? It also covers security threats and how to evaluate RAG chatbots.

Everyday versionA restaurant checks ingredients on delivery (data), follows the same recipe every time (pipeline), tastes each dish (model), makes sure the waiters and kitchen work together (system), and tries a new dish on a few tables before the full menu (canary).

why.html:
• Normal software fails from bugs; ML also fails from drift, corrupted data and biased data.
  • A model can score 95% overall and still fail half of one user group.
  • Offline tests can't prove real business impact.

how.title: Agents as a film crew
how.html: One director doing every job (a giant if/else loop) is fragile. A crew of specialists, each a subclass of a base crew member, each in its own bubble, all told "Execute!", is easy to extend: add a sound engineer without touching anyone else.

how.title: What to test in ML
how.html: Data tests (schemas, missing values, distributions), model tests (performance, fairness, edge cases), infrastructure tests (API load and latency) and heuristic tests (common sense like age ≥ 0). Many fast tests at the bottom of the pyramid, a few end-to-end tests at the top.

how.title: The MLOps loop
how.html: Data → validation → feature store → training → registry and CI/CD → deployment → monitoring → retraining, round and round. Pipelines should be idempotent (rerun gives the same result), versioned and orchestrated (Airflow, Kubeflow); CI runs tests, a quick training smoke test and schema checks on every change.

how.title: Check the data at the door
how.html: Good data is accurate, complete, consistent and timely. Pass every batch through gates (schema, values, labels) and stop the pipeline if too much fails, instead of training on garbage.

how.title: Beyond accuracy: slice it
how.html: Use precision, recall, F1 or RMSE as the problem needs. Then check accuracy per group (device, region, gender): a model that's 95% overall can be 48% for mobile users. Training tests check learning; inference tests check speed, formats and stability.

how.title: The model is <5% of the system
how.html: A perfect model behind a broken app is worth nothing. Watch system metrics (CPU, latency), model metrics (prediction distribution, confidence) and business metrics (clicks, conversions), with alerts.

how.title: Try it on real traffic, safely
how.html: A/B: split users between old and new to measure impact. Shadow: new model sees a copy of traffic but nobody gets its answers. Canary: start with 1% of users and grow if all is well.

how.title: Security threats
how.html: Attackers can poison training data, hide a backdoor in the model, slip in a bad library, fool the model with crafted inputs, or copy it by querying the API. Think about threats from day one.

demo.html: Pick a failure and see which of the four RAG metrics catches it: faithfulness and answer relevance grade the generator, context precision and context recall grade the retriever.

example.html:
A loan model release. Nightly data passes schema, value and label gates; one night 40% of records have a new date format and the pipeline halts with an alert instead of retraining. The candidate model beats the champion overall but fails the "self-employed" slice, so it isn't promoted. A later version runs in shadow for a week, then as a 1% canary, then in a 50/50 A/B test that shows a 2% increase in approved good loans.

Supplementary LLM judges have biases (preferring longer answers, for example); check them against a small set of human labels.

misunderstandings: If the code tests pass, the ML system is fine.
Data, model and system can all fail with correct code.
High global accuracy means the model works for everyone.
Shadow testing tells you how users react.
Users never see shadow outputs; use A/B for impact.
They can't detect hallucination or bad retrieval.
takeaways: ML tests: data, model, infrastructure, heuristic; pyramid from unit to system tests.
Validate data with gates and halt on failure; quality dimensions: accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness.
Pipelines must be idempotent, versioned and covered by CI.
Use the right metrics and slice them; test training and inference differently; monitor system, model and business telemetry.
Release with A/B, shadow or canary; guard against poisoning, backdoors, supply-chain, evasion and model stealing; evaluate RAG with faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision and recall.
thirty: ML testing differs from traditional testing because logic is learned: tests must cover the learning process, data integrity and statistical outputs, since failures come from drift, corrupted data and bias. Data, model, infrastructure and heuristic tests form a pyramid from unit tests to system tests, inside an MLOps loop of validation, training, registry, deployment, monitoring and retraining. Data validation uses schema, value and label gates with a halting action gateway; pipelines are idempotent, versioned and run in CI. Model quality uses precision, recall, F1 or RMSE, sliced by subgroup. Training and inference are tested differently, and system, model and business telemetry is monitored. New models are released through A/B, shadow or canary routing; security covers poisoning, backdoors, supply-chain attacks, evasion and model stealing. RAG is evaluated with RAGAS: faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision and context recall.
